1.note: Here, **Ephraim** represents the people who were leaders of the northern kingdom of Israel, since Ephraim was its largest and most prominent tribe. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the leaders of the northern kingdom of Israel]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trembling**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [people trembled in fear]

The speaker is speaking of people exalting themselves and being proud or arrogant as if they had physically **lifted up** themselves. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He exalted himself] or [He became proud of himself]

The implication is that, by worshiping Baal, the people of Ephraim brought about their own destruction as a nation, as if they had **died**. Their disobedience would eventually lead to the end of the nation of Israel. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and so destroyed himself as a nation]

2.note: The pronoun **they** here going forward refers to the people of Ephraim or the northern kingdom of Israel, which is a shift from the previous verse where the nation is referred to as the person with his name and the singular pronoun**he**. Throughout this chapter, the pronouns referring to the nation vary between singular and plural. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the singular here and in the next verses or use the plural throughout as modeled in the UST. Alternate translation: [Ephraim continued to sin]

The speaker is using the possessive form to describe a **work** that is characterized by being made by **craftsmen**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is only handmade by craftsmen] or [is made by craftsmen]

2.q: לָ⁠הֶם֙ הֵ֣ם אֹמְרִ֔ים זֹבְחֵ֣י אָדָ֔ם עֲגָלִ֖ים יִשָּׁקֽוּ⁠ן
2.note: The pronoun **them** could refer to: (1) the idols. Then the pronoun **they** would refer to the **sacrificers**, that is, those who offer sacrifices to the idols. Alternate translation: [Those people who sacrifice humans talk to the idols; they kiss the calves] or (2) the **sacrificers**, and then the pronoun **they** would refer to people in general who are talking about the sacrificers. In this case, the word translated as **saying** would introduce a quote of what these people were saying. Alternate translation: [Of the sacrificers people are saying, “Sacrificers of humans, they kiss calves!”]

3.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a cloud** and **the dew** that appears early in the day disappears as the day goes on, so the people of Ephraim will soon disappear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like a morning cloud and the early dew that quickly vanishes]

The point of this comparison is that just as **chaff** is quickly blown away from the threshing floor and is worthless, so the people of Ephraim will be swept away. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like worthless chaff that is quickly blown away from the threshing floor]

The expression **is blown away** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language as modeled in the UST.

The point of this comparison is that just as **smoke** quickly dissipates as it goes out from a window, so the people of Ephraim will soon disappear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and like smoke that quickly disappears out the window]

4.note: This is the beginning of what Yahweh said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh as modeled in the UST. See how you translated the similar statement, “And I am Yahweh your God from the land of Egypt.” in 12:9.

5.note: Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I knew** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he is the one who cared for their ancestors. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I, Yahweh knew you]

6.note: Yahweh is speaking of the provision he gave the people as if it were **pasturage** where they fed like animals and became satisfied. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [According to the food that I provided them, they ate until they were satisfied]

Yahweh is speaking of the people becoming proud as if their **heart** were **lifted up**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly as modeled in the UST.
The term translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [As a result,]

7.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a lion** attacks its prey fiercely, so Yahweh will act fiercely toward the people in judgment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like a fierce lion attacking its prey]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a leopard** lurks beside the path to ambush its prey, so Yahweh will watch and wait for the right time to bring judgment on them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like a leopard that waits beside the path to attack, so I will watch and wait to punish them]

8.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a bereaved bear** attacks with ferocious rage when someone takes her cubs, so Yahweh will confront the people in his anger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [with the fierce rage of a bereaved bear]

Yahweh is speaking of destroying the people as if he were a wild animal that would **tear open the enclosure of their heart**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly as modeled in the UST.

The point of this comparison is that just as **a lioness** devours its prey, so Yahweh will completely destroy the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and completely destroy them as a lioness does her prey]

9.note: The pronoun **It** refers to Israel’s rebellion against Yahweh, which is described in the rest of the verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Your rebellion has destroyed you]

Here, **Israel** represents the people of the northern kingdom of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Israelites]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **help**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [against the one who helps you]

10.q: אֱהִ֤י מַלְכְּ⁠ךָ֙ אֵפ֔וֹא וְ⁠יוֹשִֽׁיעֲ⁠ךָ֖ בְּ⁠כָל־עָרֶ֑י⁠ךָ וְ⁠שֹׁ֣פְטֶ֔י⁠ךָ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אָמַ֔רְתָּ תְּנָ⁠ה־לִּ֖⁠י מֶ֥לֶךְ וְ⁠שָׂרִֽים
10.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that the people’s king is unable to save them. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Even though you asked for a king to save you and for judges to rule you, they cannot help you now.]

10.q: וְ⁠שֹׁ֣פְטֶ֔י⁠ךָ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אָמַ֔רְתָּ תְּנָ⁠ה־לִּ֖⁠י מֶ֥לֶךְ וְ⁠שָׂרִֽים
10.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and your judges that I gave you because you asked me for a king and princes?]

11.note: Yahweh is using **in my nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in my anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [even though it made me angry]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wrath**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because I am angry]

12.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional as modeled in the UST. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in poetry, and follow that approach here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [I have recorded all of the evil things that Ephraim has done]

The speaker is speaking of all of Ephraim’s sinfulness as if it were a physical object that is **bound up** and **stored up** to be kept for the future. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have remembered the iniquity of Ephraim; I have kept a record of his sin for future punishment]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The wrong things done by]

13.note: The speaker is speaking of the suffering that judgment will bring on the people as if it were **pains of a woman giving birth**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Intense suffering will come to him]

The speaker is using the possessive form to describe a **womb opening** that is characterized by being the place through which **sons** are born. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he refused to come out at the opening where babies are born]

14.note: These phrases could be: (1) expressions of Yahweh’s frustration that he wants to redeem the people of Israel, but their sin and rebellion keep him from doing so, as in the ULT and UST, or (2) promises that Yahweh will redeem the people of Israel. Alternate translation: [From the hand of Sheol I will ransom them; from death I will redeem them] or (3) questions that expect a negative answer. Alternate translation: [From the hand of Sheol should I ransom them? No! From death should I redeem them? No]

Here, **hand** represents the power or grip of Sheol, the place of the dead. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [From the power of death]

14.q: אֱהִ֨י דְבָרֶי⁠ךָ֜ מָ֗וֶת אֱהִ֤י קָֽטָבְ⁠ךָ֙ שְׁא֔וֹל
14.note: Yahweh is speaking to **Death** and **Sheol**, which he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly that they deserve death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Death and Sheol. Alternate translation: [Where are the plague and destruction that bring death]

14.q: אֱהִ֨י דְבָרֶי⁠ךָ֜ מָ֗וֶת אֱהִ֤י קָֽטָבְ⁠ךָ֙ שְׁא֔וֹל
14.note: The meaning of these two questions could be: (1) that Yahweh is calling on Death to bring out its plagues and for Sheol to bring out its destructive forces. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [Bring your plagues, Death! Bring your destruction, Sheol!] or (2) that the plagues of Death and the destruction of Sheol are nowhere to be found. If you decided to translate the first two phrases of this verse as promises that Yahweh will redeem the people of Israel, then you may want to choose this option. Alternate translation: [Your plagues have gone missing, Death! Your destruction is gone, Sheol!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **your destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your power to destroy]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if his **Relenting** toward Israel were a thing that could be **hidden from my eyes**, out of his sight so that he could not act on it. He means that he will not change his mind and show mercy to Israel. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will not change my mind about this]

15.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Ephraim. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Ephraim, among brothers, he bears fruit]

The speaker is speaking of Ephraim prospering more than the other tribes as if he were a plant that **bears fruit**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in comparison to his brothers, he prospers]

The speaker is speaking of the destructive judgment of the enemies from the east that Yahweh will send, **the wind of Yahweh**, as if it were **an easterly**, a scorching wind from the east. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a destroyer sent by Yahweh will come]

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way as in the UST. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [and his fountain will dry up, indeed his spring as well]

The word translated as **will be ashamed** is a translation of the written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. Scholars suggest that two letters got switched from the original reading, which was the word meaning “will dry up.” The ancient Greek and Syriac translations also translated the word as “will dry up.” Alternate translation: [and his fountain will dry up]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **It** separately, even though the verb translated as **it will plunder** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize how completely the enemies will plunder them. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [They will completely plunder]

The speaker is using the possessive form to describe a **vessel** that is characterized by being desirable and valuable. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [every desirable possession]

16.note: Here, **Samaria** represents the people who live in the city of Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The people living in Samaria]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since Samaria has rebelled against her God, she will bear guilt]

16.q: מָרְתָ֖ה בֵּֽ⁠אלֹהֶ֑י⁠הָ בַּ⁠חֶ֣רֶב יִפֹּ֔לוּ עֹלְלֵי⁠הֶ֣ם יְרֻטָּ֔שׁוּ וְ⁠הָרִיּוֹתָ֖י⁠ו
16.note: The pronouns **she**, **her**, **they**, **their**, and **his** all refer to the people of Samaria. Throughout this verse, the pronouns vary between singular and plural and even gender. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the singular masculine pronouns as is more common for consistency or use the plural throughout as modeled in the UST. Alternate translation: [he has rebelled against his God. By the sword he will fall; his young children will be dashed to pieces, and his pregnant women]

Here, **the sword** represents warfare and violent death in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [They will die in battle]
The pronoun **they** refers to the people of Samaria. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the people of Samaria will fall]

The expression **will be dashed to pieces** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [their enemies will dash their young children to pieces]

The expression **will be ripped open** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and their enemies will cut open their pregnant women]
